routes.description: Establish a historically grounded account of Jesus as the bearer of God's nonviolent kingdom, distinguish theological interpretation from recoverable event claims, and explain divine identity and resurrection as reality-forming metaphor expressed through communal participation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources warrant Jesus's kingdom-centered and nonviolent mission while leaving literal divine preexistence and bodily rising historically unverified, and if metaphorical resurrection coherently accounts for vindication, transformed life, and collective hope.

motionBridge.description: Connect the historically recoverable Jesus and the limits of the sources to a coherent metaphorical account of divine identity and resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Show that Gospel redaction, dependence, and theological variation limit confident recovery of eyewitness testimony and literal event claims.
Ground Jesus's identity in his enacted proclamation of God's present kingdom, justice, and nonviolence rather than literal personal preexistence.
Explain resurrection as God's vindication of Jesus and a collective, participatory transformation that is not exhausted by bodily mechanics.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish historical investigation of miracle traditions and their significance from automatic acceptance of supernatural causation.
Establish that metaphor can express consequential reality and sustain allegiance, communal practice, and resistance to imperial violence.

routes.description: Establish a disciplined method for recovering facts about Jesus, defend the early and eyewitness-rooted value of the sources, and use their convergent claims about Jesus's authority, divine identity, empty tomb, appearances, and transformed body to support bodily resurrection.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if ordinary historical criteria yield reliable access to Jesus and early Christian testimony, that testimony supports extraordinary divine identity and a physical resurrection, and historical verification of the event does not require identifying its supernatural cause.

motionBridge.description: Connect historically recoverable early testimony about Jesus's identity and postmortem fate to the conclusion that he underwent bodily resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Show that source proximity, independent attestation, embarrassment, and related criteria can establish facts despite historians' differing interpretive horizons.
Show that early sayings, Pauline material, and Gospel portrayals attribute uniquely divine authority, action, or status to Jesus.
Show that early independent sources describe an empty tomb, appearances, and bodily transformation rather than only changed conduct or symbolic vindication.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish historical verification of an extraordinary event from historical identification of the event's supernatural cause.
Support access to Jesus through distributed early teaching traditions and testimony plausibly rooted in eyewitnesses.

sections.title: Historical Method and Access to Jesus
sections.rationale: The debate depends on what historical inquiry can recover despite interpretive horizons and on whether ordinary authenticity criteria provide warranted access to facts and teachings about Jesus.

sections.title: Gospel Witness, Redaction, and Independence
sections.rationale: Claims about eyewitness roots, evangelists' theological composition, literary dependence, and independent attestation determine how much evidentiary force the Gospel traditions can bear.

sections.title: Jesus's Kingdom Mission and Divine Identity
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparing a kingdom-centered, nonviolent account of Jesus with claims that early sources portray him as preexistent, divinely authoritative, and the eschatological judge.

sections.title: Miracles and Extraordinary-Event Inference
sections.rationale: The parties dispute how historians should interpret healings and raisings, whether reported extraordinary events remain historically investigable, and whether event verification can be separated from causal explanation.

sections.title: Bodily and Metaphorical Resurrection
sections.rationale: The principal clash concerns whether the earliest resurrection traditions warrant a physical transformation of Jesus or a collective, participatory metaphor of vindication and transformed life.
